nameStory: The Plum Finger Gall Mite gets its name from the peculiar finger-like galls it creates on plum and cherry trees. These swollen, elongated growths stick out from leaves like tiny green or reddish fingers, each one home to hundreds of microscopic mites. The word 'gall' comes from the Latin 'galla,' meaning an abnormal plant growth caused by insects or mites.
description: The Plum Finger Gall Mite is a microscopic arachnid so tiny you'll never see the actual mite without a powerful microscope - they're only about 0.2mm long! What you will notice are the distinctive finger-like galls they create on plum, cherry, and other stone fruit trees. These mites are pale yellow to translucent and have only four legs (unlike most arachnids), with elongated, worm-like bodies that help them move through plant tissues.

idTips.label: Gall Shape
idTips.description: Look for finger-like projections sticking out from leaf surfaces - they feel firm and slightly rubbery when gently squeezed, ranging from green to reddish-purple

idTips.label: Host Plants
idTips.description: Found exclusively on plum, cherry, and related stone fruit trees (Prunus species) - never on other tree types

idTips.label: Gall Texture
idTips.description: Galls have a smooth, waxy surface that feels slightly sticky to the touch, unlike the fuzzy or bumpy galls made by other mites

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual galls are typically 5-15mm long and 2-4mm wide, about the size of a small grain of rice

idTips.label: Arrangement
idTips.description: Galls usually appear in clusters of 3-12 on a single leaf, often concentrated along the leaf edges or major veins

habitat: Found throughout New England wherever wild or cultivated plum and cherry trees grow, from backyard orchards to forest edges. They're particularly common in disturbed areas, old farmsteads, and along woodland borders where wild cherry and plum trees thrive. You'll spot their galls from sea level to mid-elevation forests, anywhere their host trees can establish.

seasonality.spring: Adult mites emerge from overwintering sites in tree bark and begin creating new galls as leaves unfurl. Early galls appear as small bumps that quickly elongate into finger shapes.
seasonality.summer: Peak gall development occurs, with finger-like projections reaching full size and turning various shades of green, yellow, or reddish-purple. Multiple generations develop inside the protective galls.
seasonality.fall: Galls begin to dry out and turn brown as mites prepare for winter. Some galls may persist on trees even after leaves drop, becoming papery and brittle.
seasonality.winter: Adult mites shelter in bark crevices and bud scales. Old galls from the previous year can still be found as dried, brown structures on bare branches.

funFact: A single finger gall can house over 1,000 individual mites living together in a complex society, with some mites specialized for reproduction while others focus on expanding and maintaining their shared home - it's like a microscopic apartment building!
confusionNotes: The finger-like galls are sometimes mistaken for fungal infections or insect damage, but true galls always have a hollow interior chamber and smooth exterior. If you cut one open (gently!), you'll see the hollow space where mites live - fungal growths are solid throughout.
contextualKnowledge: These mites belong to a group called eriophyid mites, which are unique among arachnids for having only four legs instead of the typical eight. Despite being called 'gall mites,' they're more closely related to dust mites than to spiders, and they represent some of the smallest arachnids on Earth.
compareHints: Unlike the Red Nail Gall Mite that creates short, nail-like bumps on linden trees, the Plum Finger Gall Mite makes much longer, more cylindrical projections. The Black Cherry Leaf Gall Mite causes leaf curling and rolling rather than distinct finger projections. Each Eriophyes species is highly host-specific, so the tree type is your best clue for identification.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike the Red Nail Gall Mite that creates elongated, finger-like projections on linden leaves, or the Pearleaf Blister Mite that forms reddish blisters on fruit trees, the Black Cherry Leaf Gall Mite creates distinctly rounded, bump-like galls.

Red Nail Gall Mites create the most dramatically shaped galls in their genus - while relatives like the Lime Felt Gall Mite create fuzzy patches and others make simple bumps or blisters, only tiliae produces these unmistakable nail or horn-shaped protrusions.

While many Eriophyes species create galls on different trees, the Alder Leaf Gall Mite's small, simple dome-shaped galls are quite different from relatives like the Red Nail Gall Mite that creates finger-like projections on linden leaves, or the Pearleaf Blister Mite that causes broad, blistered areas rather than distinct bumps.
Unlike its relatives that create nail-shaped galls on linden trees or finger-like projections on cherry leaves, the Birch Leaf Gall Mite creates relatively simple bumps and fuzzy patches.
Eriophyes rhoinus differs from its relatives primarily by its host plant preference for sumac species, while other Eriophyes mites specialize on different trees like cherry, maple, or alder.

While many Eriophyes mites in New England create galls on different trees, the Lime Felt Gall Mite is unique in producing that characteristic felt texture - its close relative the Red Nail Gall Mite makes hard, nail-like projections on linden leaves, while others like the Black Cherry Leaf Gall Mite create smooth pouches.
Unlike other Eriophyes species that target maples, cherries, or birches, this species is exclusively found on viburnums.
Unlike the Black Cherry Leaf Gall Mite that creates elongated finger-like projections, the Maple Gall Mite produces rounder, more dome-shaped galls.

Eriophyes leionotus differs from its relatives primarily by its specific host plant preferences and gall characteristics rather than the mite's appearance, since all Eriophyes species look remarkably similar under magnification.
Unlike its relatives that create nail-like projections (Red Nail Gall Mite) or finger-shaped growths (Plum Finger Gall Mite), the Serviceberry Gall Mite creates more subtle, pouch-like swellings.

Unlike other Eriophyes mites that create finger-like projections (like Plum Finger Gall Mite) or felt-like patches (like Lime Felt Gall Mite), the Pearleaf Blister Mite creates smooth, dome-shaped blisters.

Unlike its relatives that create felt-like patches (Lime Felt Gall Mite) or target fruit trees (Pearleaf Blister Mite), the lime gall mite creates distinct raised bumps specifically on basswood leaves.

Unlike the Black Cherry Leaf Gall Mite which creates smooth, nail-like projections, or the Lime Felt Gall Mite which makes dense, hair-like patches, this species creates more irregularly-shaped, moderately fuzzy galls.
